Messages.Author: Cantila
Messages.Body:
DI: If player A bleeds and player B tries to block, A plays stealth
and B plays DI to cancel it, can player B now change blocker or does
the original blocking minion have to block the action? This discussion
happened last night, my guess is that player B cannot change blocker
but we would like to know for sure.

Bundi: As it says "strike:...." does it mean that you cannot strike
with Bundi with an Undead Strength? As they're two separate strikes,
unlike with a Bastard Swiord for example that merely gives +1 strength
on strikes?

Messages.Author: LSJ
Messages.Body:
Cantila wrote:
> DI: If player A bleeds and player B tries to block, A plays stealth
> and B plays DI to cancel it, can player B now change blocker or does
> the original blocking minion have to block the action? This discussion
> happened last night, my guess is that player B cannot change blocker
> but we would like to know for sure.

Correct, you can't just decide to stop a currently-succeeding block attempt.

> Bundi: As it says "strike:...." does it mean that you cannot strike
> with Bundi with an Undead Strength? As they're two separate strikes,
> unlike with a Bastard Swiord for example that merely gives +1 strength
> on strikes?

No, it doesn't mean that. All weapons say "strike...". Card text on Undead
Strength allows it to be used with a weapon.

Messages.Author: PaulW...@gmail.com
Messages.Body:
> > Bundi: As it says "strike:...." does it mean that you cannot strike
> > with Bundi with an Undead Strength? As they're two separate strikes,
> > unlike with a Bastard Swiord for example that merely gives +1 strength
> > on strikes?
>
> No, it doesn't mean that. All weapons say "strike...". Card text on Undead
> Strength allows it to be used with a weapon.

Is this correct? To me it looks like the strike is a hand/melee weapon
strike with +1 strength striking for 2 (with a basic vampire). If you
strike with undead strength you make another strike for +1/+2 strength
striking for 2 or 3 even if you have the Bundi equipped. Also not all
melee weapons say "Strike:..." for instance: Bang Nakh says "Strength
+2 damage each strike", Banshee Ironwall: "Strength +2 damage each
strike", Bastard Sword: "Strength +1 damage each strike", Black
Gloves: "Strenght +1 aggravated damage each strike" and on and on

All those weapons don't have the wording "Strike:..." and can therefor
be used in conjunction with undead strength.

Or am I mistaken, and if so, please explain why all those weapons
don't have the strike:.. wording on them and why for example even
Talith (which came out in the same set) doesn't have that wording.

Messages.Author: Thrall of Arika
Messages.Body:


I think LSJ would know if it is correct, yes. :)

The wording on Bundi is more just extra text to ensure card clarity.
All weapons are inherently Strike cards when they are used to strike.
So in effect all are "Strike: card text" ... "strength + 1 damage each
strike" is equivalent to "strike: strength + 1 damage".

In any case, the wording on Undead Strength and similar cards allows
for use on Bundi and similarly worded weapons (Argent Baton, Garotte,
Nightstick). More than likely, the wording is more precise on these
cards because of their additional effects and to avoid any unnecessary
confusion.

Undead Strength
[pot] Strike: hand strike or use a melee weapon strike. This strike is
at +1 damage.
[POT] Strike: hand strike or use a melee weapon strike. This strike is
at +2 damage.

Since striking with Bundi is a melee weapon strike, by it's own card
text, Undead Strength allows you to use that weapon strike at +1/+2
damage.

Not also that cards such as Undead Strength apply to Melee Weapons.
They won't affect Gun strikes, nor merely Weapons such as Talbot's
Chainsaw. And if the inherent strike does no damage, there is no
damage to enhance (Rowan Ring, for example).

Chris, Thrall of Arika

"That wording"?

Argent Baton

and, even:

Talith (Ravnos alt. use)

> and all other non-weapon strike cards who have
> such similar wording restricts you from using another strike card
> together with it.

> Which is why I thought Talith etc were worded the
> way they were and Bundi doesn't fit into that.

I think this is the bit that is confusing you -- the idea that "strike: blah"
texts are somehow self-restrictive while weapons' texts (other than the "strike:
blah" templated ones) are not.

Those "strike: blah" texts are not self-restrictive (just like weapons are not
self-restrictive). "Strike: blah" is not self-restrictive (except by way of
identifying the effect as a strike, just as "blah as a strike" or "blah each
strike" identifies the effect as a strike).

Granted, there are few strike cards that permit the use of other generic strikes
(as opposed to weapons, for which there are many other strike cards that permit
their use).

> If Bundi was worded the
> way it is to avoid confusion it failed miserably :P

What would have been the proper wording?

"Hand strike for strength+1 damage each strike"?

Perhaps, but that

1) means exactly what the current text means
while
2) being more stilted and equally clear/confusing (if approached honestly).

> It's the wording
> as it is now that causes confusion if anythng. Had it been worded like
> other melee weapons it'd all been crystal clear IMO.

Other melee weapons don't generate the Bundi effect, so wording it like them
would mean changing the design of Bundi.

Messages.Author: Thrall of Arika
Messages.Body:


Perhaps it's just me, but I never saw the confusion around "Strike:
<blah>" and "<blah> each strike". The only thing I could possibly see
is that one might think that the "Strike:" part limits the card to one
use per action, which it doesn't. A weapon needs specific text _to_
limit it, i.e. Chainsaw, Gas-powered Chainsaw and Sawed-off Shotgun.
Even then, the wording 'each strike' doesn't lead any more logically
to being able to be used multiple times in a combat. If a weapon could
only be used once for it's effect, we wouldn't have wording such as
for Brass Knuckles - "Strength+1 damage each strike, only usable once
each combat."

Keep in mind that Bundi is also a _hand_ strike, not merely a weapon
strike. Seeing LSJ's alternate wording makes me, as an editor, tremble
in horror. Personally, I prefer the "Strike: <blah>" wording, as it's
more concise, and parallels wording on combat strike cards (which are
by default one use only, unless card text says otherwise).

Chris, Thrall of Arika

Messages.Author: Meej
Messages.Body:
On Feb 29, 12:40 pm, Thrall of Arika <christopher.ack...@amec.com>
wrote:

> Perhaps it's just me, but I never saw the confusion around "Strike:
> <blah>" and "<blah> each strike".

Well, not that I'm actually confused by it, but I'm definitely one of
the folks who's been (and still is) extremely bothered by the
templating, and especially by the fact that, even within the same set,
it's not consistently applied. (See Bundi vs. Talith, and even Talith
vs. Talith.)

"<fnord> each strike" is text that, to me, tells you what the results
are when you use the item in question as a strike. The rules grant
you specific options to strike with your hand, a weapon, or a strike
from a card effect, whether combat or other. Certain card effects,
like Undead Strength, might allow you to use their Strike with either
your hand or a melee weapon as the base.

"Strike: <fnord>" is text that, to me, implies you're choosing to use
that particular Strike *as* your strike. You only get one of those in
each Choose Strike phase. You can't Undead Strength and Slam in the
same choose strike phase.

It seems, to me, very very counterintuitive to say "You only get one
Strike: <fnord> effect, unless that effect says you can use a hand or
weapon strike and you choose a weapon that's also written as Strike:
<fnord>." Saying you can Undead Strength with a Strike: <fnord>
weapon also leaves the implication that you could Undead Strength with
a Slam. After all, they're both the same template. Sure, you can't
US:Slam by *ruling* (or, more accurately, you *can* US:<Bundi> by
ruling), but that's not as clean as it could be.

Regarding proper alternate wording for Bundi:
"Melee weapon. Strength + 1 damage each strike. Any strike made with
a Bundi is both a hand strike and a melee weapon strike. Bearer may
prevent 1 damage from each melee weapon strike made against him or
her."

Only 4 words longer, and clearer, IMO.

- D.J.

Messages.Author: LSJ
Messages.Body:
Meej wrote:
> On Feb 29, 12:40 pm, Thrall of Arika <christopher.ack...@amec.com>
> wrote:
>
>> Perhaps it's just me, but I never saw the confusion around "Strike:
>> <blah>" and "<blah> each strike".
>
> Well, not that I'm actually confused by it, but I'm definitely one of
> the folks who's been (and still is) extremely bothered by the
> templating, and especially by the fact that, even within the same set,
> it's not consistently applied. (See Bundi vs. Talith, and even Talith
> vs. Talith.)
>
> "<fnord> each strike" is text that, to me, tells you what the results
> are when you use the item in question as a strike.
>

> "Strike: <fnord>" is text that, to me, implies you're choosing to use
> that particular Strike *as* your strike.

Well, assuming you're not saying that having the equipment automatically forces
you to choose it as your strike, the two things you've said above are
equivalent: that <fnord> is what happens when you choose the particular item in
question as your strike.

> It seems, to me, very very counterintuitive to say "You only get one
> Strike: <fnord> effect, unless that effect says you can use a hand or
> weapon strike and you choose a weapon that's also written as Strike:
> <fnord>." Saying you can Undead Strength with a Strike: <fnord>
> weapon also leaves the implication that you could Undead Strength with
> a Slam. After all, they're both the same template. Sure, you can't
> US:Slam by *ruling* (or, more accurately, you *can* US:<Bundi> by
> ruling), but that's not as clean as it could be.

Incorrect.

Undead Strength + Weapon text application:

US: Strike: use a melee weapon strike.
So then, as per the US text, you choose a melee weapon and use its strike.

Undead Strength + Slam text application:

US: Strike: hand strike.
So then, your strike is "hand strike" and you're done. You don't get to choose Slam.

Note the difference. The Undead Strength's hand strike part doesn't say "use
a(ny) hand strike at...", it just says "Hand strike".

> Regarding proper alternate wording for Bundi:
> "Melee weapon. Strength + 1 damage each strike. Any strike made with
> a Bundi is both a hand strike and a melee weapon strike. Bearer may
> prevent 1 damage from each melee weapon strike made against him or
> her."
>
> Only 4 words longer, and clearer, IMO.

4 words longer. Perhaps clearer. Perhaps less clear. (As text may be read such
that the strike isn't a hand strike until it is made, can it be used under
Grapple?, for example, would be one question that is arguably less clear with
that wording than with the current).

Messages.Body:

I can see what you mean. What I was trying to express was the
following: replace "as" with "during" in the "fnord each strike"
description. Given that, can you see the distinction I'm seeing?

If not, still, let me put it a little differently. "When you use
<foo> it does <bar>" implies, to me, a variety of methods of using
<foo> (Strength +1 damage each strike). "Use <foo> to do <bar>"
implies, to me, that you get <bar> from your <foo> when used in
exactly that way (Strike: Strength +1 damage). Yes, those are not the
precise language used on the cards, and I recognize that that makes a
difference, but if precise language is that important, why is the
templating inconsistent?

> > It seems, to me, very very counterintuitive to say "You only get one
> > Strike: <fnord> effect, unless that effect says you can use a hand or
> > weapon strike and you choose a weapon that's also written as Strike:
> > <fnord>." Saying you can Undead Strength with a Strike: <fnord>
> > weapon also leaves the implication that you could Undead Strength with
> > a Slam. After all, they're both the same template. Sure, you can't
> > US:Slam by *ruling* (or, more accurately, you *can* US:<Bundi> by
> > ruling), but that's not as clean as it could be.
>
> Incorrect.

That it's not as clean as it could be? That it could leave that
implication by printed card text?
If what you mean is that it's not the same templating, or that it's by
ruling, I'll grant those - it's by online-issued clarification and (in
a few cases, I'm guessing) MRP, which technically are a slightly
different category of card text change rather than ruling.

> Undead Strength + Weapon text application:
>
> US: Strike: use a melee weapon strike.
> So then, as per the US text, you choose a melee weapon and use its strike.

Some of them don't have "Strike:"s. They have added damage when used,
sure. The rulebook allows you to use a melee weapon in a strike,
sure. But the weapon doesn't have a strike in and of itself, does
it? If the rulebook didn't say you could use a weapon without a
Strike: card, would you be able to? A gun (any of them) doesn't
specify a strike, it just says what it does when used as a strike,
like with Projectile (or, currently, with the base rules) - how would
you use it without one, if the rules only gave you the option of hand
strikes, or card plays?

(Yes, I'm being incredibly pedantic here, for the sake of a point: Why
are some weapons set up one way, and some another? Especially given
that the more-confusing version is a later addition, as far as I can
tell?)

> Undead Strength + Slam text application:
>
> US: Strike: hand strike.
> So then, your strike is "hand strike" and you're done. You don't get to choose Slam.
>
> Note the difference. The Undead Strength's hand strike part doesn't say "use
> a(ny) hand strike at...", it just says "Hand strike".

Thanks for pointing that out. (Worth noting that that's via online
clarification, since most of the strike cards with this situation in
print actually read "Make a hand or melee weapon strike at...," but
that's not a valid point of contention). Still, I can't see why you'd
set it up that way, to be honest. It seems, to me, to be cleaner to
have weapons tell their damage when used in a strike, the way it was
set up until a few sets back, rather than use Strike: formatting
exactly as on combat cards; Strike: formatting on non-combat cards
seems to me to be a great tool for making it clear when something
cannot (or, by its omission, can) be combined with other Strike:s.
(For instance, Talith's weapon-breaking, or Nightstick's damage-
prevention. Is the intent really that I can Undead Strength: Prevent
Damage with a Nightstick to do no damage, but cycle the card anyway?)

> > Regarding proper alternate wording for Bundi:
> > "Melee weapon. Strength + 1 damage each strike. Any strike made with
> > a Bundi is both a hand strike and a melee weapon strike. Bearer may
> > prevent 1 damage from each melee weapon strike made against him or
> > her."
>
> > Only 4 words longer, and clearer, IMO.
>
> 4 words longer. Perhaps clearer. Perhaps less clear.

Hence the IMO.

> (As text may be read such
> that the strike isn't a hand strike until it is made, can it be used under
> Grapple?, for example, would be one question that is arguably less clear with
> that wording than with the current).

Good catch. 3 words longer, then, and remove "made." I can't see how
that is arguably less clear anymore.

Honestly, LSJ - I'm not arguing that anything currently possible
should be switched to be impossible, or that anything currently
impossible should be switched to be possible, and I'm not disputing
that the rulings, clarifications, whatever, work. I was answering
Chris's question about what the issue raised in the past was.

And to be honest, I'm continuing with it because, generally, you've
shown yourself to be in favor of cleaner, less-confusing, more-
consistent card text, and this is one of the few cases where it seems
to me that the logical inferences from the card text distinctions run
counter to the way you're looking at it.

- D.J.

Messages.Author: LSJ
Messages.Body:
Meej wrote:
> I can see what you mean. What I was trying to express was the
> following: replace "as" with "during" in the "fnord each strike"
> description. Given that, can you see the distinction I'm seeing?
>
> If not, still, let me put it a little differently. "When you use
> <foo> it does <bar>" implies, to me, a variety of methods of using
> <foo> (Strength +1 damage each strike).

What variety? "Strength +1 damage each strike" is not a variety. It's one
effect. An effect that happens to be a strike.

> "Use <foo> to do <bar>"
> implies, to me, that you get <bar> from your <foo> when used in
> exactly that way (Strike: Strength +1 damage).

True. That's also what "When you use <foo> it does <bar>" implies.

> Yes, those are not the
> precise language used on the cards, and I recognize that that makes a
> difference, but if precise language is that important, why is the
> templating inconsistent?

Different effects sometimes require (or at least, benefit from) different templates.

>> Undead Strength + Weapon text application:
>>
>> US: Strike: use a melee weapon strike.
>> So then, as per the US text, you choose a melee weapon and use its strike.
>
> Some of them don't have "Strike:"s.

But all weapons have strikes.

> They have added damage when used,
> sure.

You omitted the word "strike" there: "They have added damage when used to strike."

Technically, the "added damage" is just inherent damage (and is only "added" in
the sense that the inherent amount is computed by adding some value to the
bearer's strength).

So it would be more proper to say: "They inflict some specified amount of damage
with their strikes" or, more concisely: "Their strikes inflict some specified
amount of damage".

> The rulebook allows you to use a melee weapon in a strike,
> sure. But the weapon doesn't have a strike in and of itself, does
> it?

Yes, the weapon has a strike. That is, it has a strike effect that occurs when
it is used as a strike.

> If the rulebook didn't say you could use a weapon without a
> Strike: card, would you be able to?

No. Having a strike effect is not the same as having a strike opportunity,
although "has a strike" can be used to mean either, depending on context.

> A gun (any of them) doesn't
> specify a strike, it just says what it does when used as a strike,

Same thing.

> like with Projectile (or, currently, with the base rules) - how would
> you use it without one, if the rules only gave you the option of hand
> strikes, or card plays?

I don't know. Fortunately, it's moot, since the rules don't "only give the
option of hand strikes or card plays".

Rulebook: "Choose Strike. Each minion chooses his strike. The strike can be from
a combat card, from a weapon the minion possesses or (the default) from a hand
strike." [6.4.3]

> (Yes, I'm being incredibly pedantic here, for the sake of a point: Why
> are some weapons set up one way, and some another? Especially given
> that the more-confusing version is a later addition, as far as I can
> tell?)

To be pedantic: specifying the effect something has when used as a strike and
specifying the strike effect for which something can be used are exactly the
same thing.

Some weapons use the alternate "Strike: <blah>" template when the effect being
described warrants it.

> It seems, to me, to be cleaner to
> have weapons tell their damage when used in a strike, the way it was
> set up until a few sets back, rather than use Strike: formatting
> exactly as on combat cards;

The Strike: formatting tells what the weapon does when used in a strike.

> Strike: formatting on non-combat cards
> seems to me to be a great tool for making it clear when something
> cannot (or, by its omission, can) be combined with other Strike:s.

Perhaps, but only if some additional rules text said it did (make the strike
unable to be combined). Since, currently, the rules don't support that notion
(and instead allow card text such as Undead Strength's to specify that a
modified weapon's strike can be used).

> (For instance, Talith's weapon-breaking, or Nightstick's damage-
> prevention. Is the intent really that I can Undead Strength: Prevent
> Damage with a Nightstick to do no damage, but cycle the card anyway?)

Moot. We're discussion effect, not intent. Is the intent of Wake really that I
can play it without attempting to block and without attempting to play another
reaction card?

> And to be honest, I'm continuing with it because, generally, you've
> shown yourself to be in favor of cleaner, less-confusing, more-
> consistent card text, and this is one of the few cases where it seems
> to me that the logical inferences from the card text distinctions run
> counter to the way you're looking at it.

It still seems to be running the correct way to me.

As far as I can tell, Undead Strength says "Make a hand or melee
weapon strike at +1/2 damage" (most recent printing). There may be
some ruling that changes the text to say what you say above, which is
fine. It's not that anyone is disputing that Undead Strength + Bundi
works different from Undead Strength + Slam (or whatever other hand
strike). It's just it doesn't *look* different per card text. Per
card text, Undead Strength says "Make a hand or melee weapon strike at
+1/2 damage." Bundi says "Strike: hand strike for strength+1 damage."
whereas (let's pick a hand strike) Khabar:Honor says "Strike: strength
+3 damage." Nothing in those card texts indicates that US can be used
with Bundi but not with Khabar:Honor. Now, the text listed on the WW
page is different. Slam, frex says "Strike: hand strike for +2
damage" instead of what the card says "Strike: make a hand strike at
+2 damage", which *might* be interpreted to mean something different.
And Undead Strength says what you quote above. But it all seems
needlessly confusing. I'm not saying it shouldn't work the way you
say it does. Your ruling makes sense. But are you saying you can't
understand why people would be confused???

OK - it strikes me as being a description of how a strike, wherever it
comes from, that uses that card functions - whether the strike is
provided by a combat card (U.S.) or by the rulebook.

> > "Use <foo> to do <bar>"
> > implies, to me, that you get <bar> from your <foo> when used in
> > exactly that way (Strike: Strength +1 damage).
>
> True. That's also what "When you use <foo> it does <bar>" implies.

Not to me, clearly, or I wouldn't have made a distinction - to me, it
reads: Here's a precise Strike: that you can make with this weapon.
It implies nothing at all to me about generic uses for the weapon in a
strike. (Other than by possible precedent from the prior-used,
clearer wording, which leaves me wondering about the different
templating.)

> > Yes, those are not the
> > precise language used on the cards, and I recognize that that makes a
> > difference, but if precise language is that important, why is the
> > templating inconsistent?
>
> Different effects sometimes require (or at least, benefit from) different templates.

Sure.

Why are there different templates being used for identical effects?
Strike: 2R aggravated damage (Waxen Poetica) and 2R aggravated damage
each strike (Improvised Flamethrower). Alternately, if the "burn
after use" makes a difference, Waxen Poetica and Grenade.

*Maybe* I can concede that the Strike: Strength +1 damage is important
for the Nightstick, to make it clear that the "prevent 3 damage"
strike doesn't get +1 damage. But that very distinction implies, to
me, that you recognize that there's something different about "Strike:
<foo>" and "<Foo> each strike." I'm not saying you do, actually, but
it certainly implies that, if that's the justification.

> >> Undead Strength + Weapon text application:
>
> >> US: Strike: use a melee weapon strike.
> >> So then, as per the US text, you choose a melee weapon and use its strike.
>
> > Some of them don't have "Strike:"s.
>
> But all weapons have strikes.

Due to the rulebook, yes. More properly, all weapons have an effect
when used as a strike. Whether they all have strikes is sort of what
we're discussing here; also, whether there is a difference between
having an effect as a strike, and having a "Strike:" choice. (Or, I
suppose - since by ruling/clarification/whatever, there's currently no
difference - whether there should be, or whether there's an implied
difference overruled by r/c/w.)

> So it would be more proper to say: "They inflict some specified amount of damage
> with their strikes" or, more concisely: "Their strikes inflict some specified
> amount of damage".

True, especially when you bring guns in. "Added" was poor phrasing on
my part.
But no argument here with your clarification.

> > The rulebook allows you to use a melee weapon in a strike,
> > sure. But the weapon doesn't have a strike in and of itself, does
> > it?
>
> Yes, the weapon has a strike. That is, it has a strike effect that occurs when
> it is used as a strike.

Which seems to me to be different than having a strike. Something
else, the rulebook or combat card in this case, provides the
opportunity for the strike effect to be used, in my eyes. Unlike,
say, Bundi, which has a Strike: printed on it. Does that seem like a
purely semantic difference to you, and are you able to explain why
there's not a distinction?

> > If the rulebook didn't say you could use a weapon without a
> > Strike: card, would you be able to?
>
> No. Having a strike effect is not the same as having a strike opportunity,
> although "has a strike" can be used to mean either, depending on context.

Hmm. I'm not sure I'm clear on what you're saying - do you mean that,
barring the rules' allowance of using a weapon to strike, having
"Strike: Strength +1 damage" printed on a weapon would not allow you
to use that as a strike?

> > A gun (any of them) doesn't
> > specify a strike, it just says what it does when used as a strike,
>
> Same thing.

Not at all, to me - specifying a strike means "here is a given,
single, precise strike you are now allowed, by this very card, to do,
when you have the opportunity to strike". What it does when used as a
strike, on the other hand, means "whenever you use this as a strike,
here's what it does," without expressly providing that strike.
Fortunately, the rules do, as may other card effects.

> > like with Projectile (or, currently, with the base rules) - how would
> > you use it without one, if the rules only gave you the option of hand
> > strikes, or card plays?
>
> I don't know. Fortunately, it's moot, since the rules don't "only give the
> option of hand strikes or card plays".
>
> Rulebook: "Choose Strike. Each minion chooses his strike. The strike can be from
> a combat card, from a weapon the minion possesses or (the default) from a hand
> strike." [6.4.3]

OK. So we're on the same page that it's the rules that allow you to
choose "weapon strike" and specify a weapon, which allows the use of
weapons.

I'd argue that "combat card" should probably read "card effect" to
allow for things such as Watchtower: Wolves Feed's effect more
clearly, but that's an aside, as that does read "may strike for 2R
damage" and thus, fairly clearly, allows a strike outside the normal
rules for choosing them.

> To be pedantic: specifying the effect something has when used as a strike and
> specifying the strike effect for which something can be used are exactly the
> same thing.

How so? One includes, explicitly, a stated way of using that
something, and the other only describes its effect when it's used.

> Some weapons use the alternate "Strike: <blah>" template when the effect being
> described warrants it.

Are there any Combat cards that are, themselves, a strike (rather
than, like Improvised Tactics, allowing one later), which don't use
that template? I can't think of any... Why would some weapons
warrant the non-Strike:<blah> template, then, if all strikes can be
represented the same way?

> > It seems, to me, to be cleaner to
> > have weapons tell their damage when used in a strike, the way it was
> > set up until a few sets back, rather than use Strike: formatting
> > exactly as on combat cards;
>
> The Strike: formatting tells what the weapon does when used in a strike.

That too, yes.

> > Strike: formatting on non-combat cards
> > seems to me to be a great tool for making it clear when something
> > cannot (or, by its omission, can) be combined with other Strike:s.
>
> Perhaps, but only if some additional rules text said it did (make the strike
> unable to be combined). Since, currently, the rules don't support that notion
> (and instead allow card text such as Undead Strength's to specify that a
> modified weapon's strike can be used).

Through online clarification wording that didn't even make it into the
MRP. Prior to that, it reads "Make a hand strike or melee weapon
strike..."

I'm not saying the rules support that notion, currently.
I'm saying that even-more-careful use of formatting could intuitively
support the correct interpretation of the rules, by having one
formatting for "effect of a strike" and another for "choice of strike,
with effect" - in other words, making it clear when something can be
chosen by something else.

If the rules (6.4.3) clearly stated "Choose Strike. Each minion
chooses his strike. A minion may only use one effect that begins with
'Strike:' per strike declaration phase. The strike can be: a Strike:
from a combat card or allowed by another card effect; Strike: use a
weapon on this minion; or (the default) Strike: Hand strike," I firmly
believe that the question of whether you can use Undead Strength with
a Slam, for instance, would be clearer than currently, and provide for
cleaner templating in the future.

> > (For instance, Talith's weapon-breaking, or Nightstick's damage-
> > prevention. Is the intent really that I can Undead Strength: Prevent
> > Damage with a Nightstick to do no damage, but cycle the card anyway?)
>
> Moot. We're discussion effect, not intent. Is the intent of Wake really that I
> can play it without attempting to block and without attempting to play another
> reaction card?

OK. Is the effect really that I can Undead Strength: Prevent damage
with a Nightstick? If so, odd; I don't think I would have intuited
that it could be played that way from the cards.

> > And to be honest, I'm continuing with it because, generally, you've
> > shown yourself to be in favor of cleaner, less-confusing, more-
> > consistent card text, and this is one of the few cases where it seems
> > to me that the logical inferences from the card text distinctions run
> > counter to the way you're looking at it.
>
> It still seems to be running the correct way to me.

Sure, by ruling/interpretation, online clarification, and accepted
ambiguity. I'm not arguing that it doesn't work. I'm arguing that it
could work better and with less ambiguity needed, as well as opening
up possible predictable future options through cleaner templating.

- D.J.

Messages.Author: LSJ
Messages.Body:
Meej wrote:
> On Feb 29, 9:55 pm, LSJ <vtes...@white-wolf.com> wrote:
>> What variety? "Strength +1 damage each strike" is not a variety. It's one
>> effect. An effect that happens to be a strike.
>
> OK - it strikes me as being a description of how a strike, wherever it
> comes from, that uses that card functions - whether the strike is
> provided by a combat card (U.S.) or by the rulebook.

Yes. It is a single effect that, since it happens to be a strike, can only be
used as a strike.

>>> "Use <foo> to do <bar>"
>>> implies, to me, that you get <bar> from your <foo> when used in
>>> exactly that way (Strike: Strength +1 damage).
>> True. That's also what "When you use <foo> it does <bar>" implies.
>
> Not to me, clearly, or I wouldn't have made a distinction - to me, it

People infer all sorts of things from text, even things that the texts do not imply.

> reads: Here's a precise Strike: that you can make with this weapon.
> It implies nothing at all to me about generic uses for the weapon in a
> strike. (Other than by possible precedent from the prior-used,
> clearer wording, which leaves me wondering about the different
> templating.)

And yet, it reads: Here's a strike effect that this weapon produces. Just like
the other template reads.

> Why are there different templates being used for identical effects?
> Strike: 2R aggravated damage (Waxen Poetica) and 2R aggravated damage
> each strike (Improvised Flamethrower). Alternately, if the "burn
> after use" makes a difference, Waxen Poetica and Grenade.

Oversight.

> *Maybe* I can concede that the Strike: Strength +1 damage is important
> for the Nightstick, to make it clear that the "prevent 3 damage"
> strike doesn't get +1 damage. But that very distinction implies, to
> me, that you recognize that there's something different about "Strike:
> <foo>" and "<Foo> each strike." I'm not saying you do, actually, but
> it certainly implies that, if that's the justification.

That distinction doesn't imply that at all. I cannot see how that can be inferred.

The two templates mean exactly the same thing. The distinction of templates is
only in readability. Making a distinction (of readabilty) in no way implies a
difference of function.

>> But all weapons have strikes.
> Due to the rulebook, yes.

?

Due to card text.

Name any weapon whose card text doesn't specify a strike effect that the weapon
provides.

> More properly, all weapons have an effect
> when used as a strike.

Exactly the same; not more or less proper.

> Whether they all have strikes is sort of what
> we're discussing here;

A weapon has a strike.

See also all ammo, Baal's Bloody Talons, Strike at the True Flesh, Sword of
Nuln: "this weapon's strike".

Some have more than one strike option. Many also have maneuvers (which are,
generally, also optional). Some even have presses. And damage prevention.

> also, whether there is a difference between
> having an effect as a strike, and having a "Strike:" choice.

The weapons all grant their strikes as strike options to their bearers.

> (Or, I
> suppose - since by ruling/clarification/whatever, there's currently no
> difference - whether there should be, or whether there's an implied
> difference overruled by r/c/w.)

There is no difference effected by the card text templates, in the absence of
the rulings/clarifications/whatever. It would take errata to change the text
function into the other more self-restrictive effect.

>>> The rulebook allows you to use a melee weapon in a strike,
>>> sure. But the weapon doesn't have a strike in and of itself, does
>>> it?
>> Yes, the weapon has a strike. That is, it has a strike effect that occurs when
>> it is used as a strike.
>
> Which seems to me to be different than having a strike.

What would it mean for a weapon to have a strike, then, other than having some
strike effect that occurs when the weapon is used as a strike?

> Something
> else, the rulebook or combat card in this case, provides the
> opportunity for the strike effect to be used, in my eyes.

The rulebook specifies when strikes can be chosen.

The "Choose Strike" phase, provided by the rulebook, is the opportunity for
minions to select strike effects to use.

The "Resolve Strike" phase, provided by the rulebook, is the opportunity for the
selected strikes to be "used".

> Unlike,
> say, Bundi, which has a Strike: printed on it.

So you say that Bundi's text provides the opportunity for the strike effect to
be used?

That's another matter altogether. If this is your argument, this whole
discussion will be much simpler. Let me know if this is the case.

> Does that seem like a
> purely semantic difference to you, and are you able to explain why
> there's not a distinction?

The explanation of why there's no difference in things that mean the same thing?

Just grammar and vocabulary. "Why" is there no difference between Bob bleeds Sue
and Sue is bled by Bob?

>>> If the rulebook didn't say you could use a weapon without a
>>> Strike: card, would you be able to?
>> No. Having a strike effect is not the same as having a strike opportunity,
>> although "has a strike" can be used to mean either, depending on context.
>
> Hmm. I'm not sure I'm clear on what you're saying - do you mean that,
> barring the rules' allowance of using a weapon to strike, having
> "Strike: Strength +1 damage" printed on a weapon would not allow you
> to use that as a strike?

The game mechanics provide the opportunity to strike. That is, minions can
strike during the strike phase of combat (and the rules also provide maneuver
opportunities, press opportunities, action declaration opportunities, and so on.
The game is just a sequence of opportunities to apply various effects.

A minion "has" one strike each round by default. But may have more than one,
given the existence of effects which produce additional strikes.

A minion also has an inherent strike. This strike (default hand strike) that he
"has" is unrelated to the "has" in the preceding paragraph.

Weapons also "have" strikes. The bearer of a weapon may use the weapon's strike
for his in-combt strike-opportunity strike, or he may use his default hand strike.

>>> A gun (any of them) doesn't
>>> specify a strike, it just says what it does when used as a strike,
>> Same thing.
>
> Not at all, to me - specifying a strike means "here is a given,
> single, precise strike you are now allowed, by this very card, to do,
> when you have the opportunity to strike".

That's exactly what the other template means, as well.

"This given, single, precise strike you are now allowed, by this very card, to
do each strike opportunity you have."

> What it does when used as a
> strike, on the other hand, means "whenever you use this as a strike,
> here's what it does," without expressly providing that strike.

?
If it doesn't provide the strike, then there's no new strike to be chosen in the
choose strike phase, so the minion would be left with just his default strike to
choose (or a strike card).

> Fortunately, the rules do, as may other card effects.

The rules do what?

Allow weapons to be used as strikes according to the strike effects listed on
their card texts?

Exactly. That is the same for both templates.

The rules say a weapon can be used to strike.
They also say that a strike card can be used.
Some strike cards specify strike whose effects are just to use a weapon (and
modify the weapon's strike in some way).

>>> like with Projectile (or, currently, with the base rules) - how would
>>> you use it without one, if the rules only gave you the option of hand
>>> strikes, or card plays?
>> I don't know. Fortunately, it's moot, since the rules don't "only give the
>> option of hand strikes or card plays".
>>
>> Rulebook: "Choose Strike. Each minion chooses his strike. The strike can be from
>> a combat card, from a weapon the minion possesses or (the default) from a hand
>> strike." [6.4.3]
>
> OK. So we're on the same page that it's the rules that allow you to
> choose "weapon strike" and specify a weapon, which allows the use of
> weapons.
>
> I'd argue that "combat card" should probably read "card effect" to
> allow for things such as Watchtower: Wolves Feed's effect more
> clearly, but that's an aside, as that does read "may strike for 2R
> damage" and thus, fairly clearly, allows a strike outside the normal
> rules for choosing them.

An aside covered by the golden rule, yes.
:-)

>> To be pedantic: specifying the effect something has when used as a strike and
>> specifying the strike effect for which something can be used are exactly the
>> same thing.
>
> How so? One includes, explicitly, a stated way of using that
> something, and the other only describes its effect when it's used.

How so: because they each describe the effect of the use.

(Each time you strike, you may use this weapon to) strike: (to inflict) 1R agg
damage (with this weapon)

is exactly the same as

(this weapon inflicts) 1R agg damage each strike (you use it to strike)

>> Some weapons use the alternate "Strike: <blah>" template when the effect being
>> described warrants it.
>
> Are there any Combat cards that are, themselves, a strike (rather
> than, like Improvised Tactics, allowing one later), which don't use
> that template?

"Are there any cards that use the longer template uselessly"? I hope not.

Improvised Tactics is a perfect example.

> I can't think of any... Why would some weapons
> warrant the non-Strike:<blah> template, then, if all strikes can be
> represented the same way?

Clarity, I presume.

>>> It seems, to me, to be cleaner to
>>> have weapons tell their damage when used in a strike, the way it was
>>> set up until a few sets back, rather than use Strike: formatting
>>> exactly as on combat cards;
>> The Strike: formatting tells what the weapon does when used in a strike.
>
> That too, yes.
>
>>> Strike: formatting on non-combat cards
>>> seems to me to be a great tool for making it clear when something
>>> cannot (or, by its omission, can) be combined with other Strike:s.
>> Perhaps, but only if some additional rules text said it did (make the strike
>> unable to be combined). Since, currently, the rules don't support that notion
>> (and instead allow card text such as Undead Strength's to specify that a
>> modified weapon's strike can be used).
>
> Through online clarification wording that didn't even make it into the
> MRP. Prior to that, it reads "Make a hand strike or melee weapon
> strike..."

Being clarified after the MRP, it would have been difficult to make it into the
MRP, yes. Temporis is only found in the WoD, not in this world.

The exact issue you are now picking up on was picked up on earlier and resulted
in the clarified card texts.

> I'm not saying the rules support that notion, currently.
> I'm saying that even-more-careful use of formatting could intuitively
> support the correct interpretation of the rules, by having one
> formatting for "effect of a strike" and another for "choice of strike,
> with effect" - in other words, making it clear when something can be
> chosen by something else.

Perhaps when the designers design an effect that they want to be additionally
self-restrictive, they'll use an appropriate template to convey that additional
restrictiveness. But they will undoubtedly not use either of the current
templates, since neither of them accomplish that restrictiveness.

> If the rules (6.4.3) clearly stated "Choose Strike. Each minion
> chooses his strike. A minion may only use one effect that begins with
> 'Strike:' per strike declaration phase. The strike can be: a Strike:
> from a combat card or allowed by another card effect; Strike: use a
> weapon on this minion; or (the default) Strike: Hand strike," I firmly
> believe that the question of whether you can use Undead Strength with
> a Slam, for instance, would be clearer than currently, and provide for
> cleaner templating in the future.
>
>>> (For instance, Talith's weapon-breaking, or Nightstick's damage-
>>> prevention. Is the intent really that I can Undead Strength: Prevent
>>> Damage with a Nightstick to do no damage, but cycle the card anyway?)
>> Moot. We're discussion effect, not intent. Is the intent of Wake really that I
>> can play it without attempting to block and without attempting to play another
>> reaction card?
>
> OK. Is the effect really that I can Undead Strength: Prevent damage
> with a Nightstick? If so, odd; I don't think I would have intuited
> that it could be played that way from the cards.

Yes.

>>> And to be honest, I'm continuing with it because, generally, you've
>>> shown yourself to be in favor of cleaner, less-confusing, more-
>>> consistent card text, and this is one of the few cases where it seems
>>> to me that the logical inferences from the card text distinctions run
>>> counter to the way you're looking at it.
>> It still seems to be running the correct way to me.
>
> Sure, by ruling/interpretation, online clarification, and accepted
> ambiguity. I'm not arguing that it doesn't work. I'm arguing that it
> could work better and with less ambiguity needed, as well as opening
> up possible predictable future options through cleaner templating.

Except for the "accepted ambiguity" bit, yes. The current official/clarified
card text doesn't have the ambiguity you describe.

Future cards relying on such seemingly-identical-meaning templates to indicate
such different effects would be bad (unnecessarily confusing the players).

Messages.Author: Thrall of Arika
Messages.Body:
On Mar 3, 9:19 am, Meej <dj...@comcast.net> wrote:
> On Feb 29, 9:55 pm, LSJ <vtes...@white-wolf.com> wrote:
> Why are there different templates being used for identical effects?
> Strike: 2R aggravated damage (Waxen Poetica) and 2R aggravated damage
> each strike (Improvised Flamethrower).  Alternately, if the "burn
> after use" makes a difference, Waxen Poetica and Grenade.

Personally, I find the use of "each strike" for one use equipment to
be rather silly and needlessly confusing. Sawed-off Shotgun has made
more than one player I know wonder at the wording. "If I can only use
it once per combat, why does it say each strike?". I would say that
Waxen Poetica was following Grenade's wording, where it's even more
evident that "Strike: <effect>" is equivalent to "<effect> as a
strike>". There's no need to errata something just to make an old card
fit a newer wording template.

> *Maybe* I can concede that the Strike: Strength +1 damage is important
> for the Nightstick, to make it clear that the "prevent 3 damage"
> strike doesn't get +1 damage.  But that very distinction implies, to
> me, that you recognize that there's something different about "Strike:
> <foo>" and "<Foo> each strike."  I'm not saying you do, actually, but
> it certainly implies that, if that's the justification.

I think it's more that English is often an imprecise language, with
the same word having different meanings based on context. Most weapons
only have one strike effect, and so having 'each strike' doesn't
affect understanding of the card's effects. Nightstick allows for two
very different strikes.

The distinction in wording only implies that there could be confusion
and arguments arising from the use of one wording over the other. Why
slavishly follow a template that could cause confusion, when another
perfectly equivalent way of wording the effect can be used to avoid
any misunderstanding?

I personally prefer the "Strike: <effect>" template. It's clear,
concise and leaves little room for misinterpretation.

> > To be pedantic: specifying the effect something has when used as a strike and
> > specifying the strike effect for which something can be used are exactly the
> > same thing.
>
> How so?  One includes, explicitly, a stated way of using that
> something, and the other only describes its effect when it's used.

The wordings are different, in that they use different words to say
the same thing .. the effects are identical.

Take as an example, a Bastard Sword. Current text allows me to strike
with the sword for strength+1 damage. I can additional strike and
strike again with the sword for strength+1 damage.

Now if we use the Strike: template, so the Bastard Sword reads
"Strike: Strength + 1 damage."

I can strike with the sword for strenght+1 damage. I can additional
strike and strike again with the sword for strength+1 damage.

Either wording is a melee weapon strike, and so I can use Undead
Strength on it. Beyond the actual words used, I fail to see how the
template wordings are not the same thing.

> > > (For instance, Talith's weapon-breaking, or Nightstick's damage-
> > > prevention.  Is the intent really that I can Undead Strength: Prevent
> > > Damage with a Nightstick to do no damage, but cycle the card anyway?)
>
> > Moot. We're discussion effect, not intent. Is the intent of Wake really that I
> > can play it without attempting to block and without attempting to play another
> > reaction card?
>
> OK.  Is the effect really that I can Undead Strength: Prevent damage
> with a Nightstick?  If so, odd; I don't think I would have intuited
> that it could be played that way from the cards.

Not any odder than Undead Strength: Strike with Rowan Ring.

I can see what you're getting at, but there seems to be no need to
change wordings that have been around for a long time, just to have
everything follow one selected template. The "each strike" wording for
most weapons is perfectly fine, and as you seem to support, more
intuitive to game play. It's only when the potential for confusion,
especially with weapons with multiple strike options, that a different
wording template should be used, thus we have the "Strike:" for Bundi
and the like. Why errata dozens of cards to fit a new template when
it's not warrented, and isn't necessary for clarity of rulings and
interpretations?

Chris, Thrall of Arika
